results.title: Forward branch of the extended continuant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and an integer $b$, the forward branch with start index $b$ is the sequence $(F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of integers defined by $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = x_{b+n} F_{n+1} + F_n$. Its value $F_n$ is the extended continuant $K_{n-2}(x)_b$.

results.title: Backward branch of the extended continuant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and an integer $b$, the backward branch with start index $b$ is the sequence $(B_m)_{m \ge 0}$ of integers defined by $B_0 = 1$, $B_1 = 0$ and $B_{m+2} = -x_{b-1-m} B_{m+1} + B_m$. Its value $B_m$ is the extended continuant $K_{-1-m}(x)_b$ of negative order $-1-m$.

results.title: Extended continuants
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a bi-infinite integer sequence and $b$ an integer. The extended continuant $K_a(x)_b$ of order $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ with start index $b$ (the paper's $K_a(x)_b^{a+b}$) is the integer defined by $K_{-2}(x)_b = 0$, $K_{-1}(x)_b = 1$, the forward recurrence $K_a(x)_b = x_{b+a} K_{a-1}(x)_b + K_{a-2}(x)_b$ for $a \ge 0$, and the backward recurrence…

results.title: Extended continuants of order $-2$ vanish
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bi-infinite integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and every integer $b$, the extended continuant of order $-2$ with start index $b$ is zero: $K_{-2}(x)_b = 0$.

results.title: Extended continuant of order $-1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and every integer $b$, the extended continuant of $x$ of order $-1$ with start index $b$ equals $1$, that is, $K_{-1}(x)_b = 1$.

results.title: The extended continuant of order $0$ is a single term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bi-infinite integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and every integer $b$, the extended continuant of order $0$ with start index $b$ is $K_0(x)_b = x_b$.

results.title: Recurrence for extended continuants
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bi-infinite integer sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and all integers $a$ and $b$, the extended continuants $K_a(x)_b$ of order $a$ with start index $b$ satisfy $K_a(x)_b = x_{b+a} K_{a-1}(x)_b + K_{a-2}(x)_b$.

results.title: The conjugate continued fraction is not purely periodic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$, $Q$ and $D$ be integers with $D > 0$ not a perfect square and $Q > 0$, and let $\bar\alpha = (P - \sqrt{D})/Q$. Then the simple continued fraction $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ of $\bar\alpha$, which is infinite because $\bar\alpha$ is irrational, is not purely periodic: there is no integer $s \ge 1$ with $a_{n+s} = a_n$ for all $n \ge 0$. Here $a_0 = \lfloor \bar\alpha \rfloor$ is included.

results.title: Blanksby–Montgomery lower bound for the Mahler measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonzero complex number that is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ and is not a root of unity, and let $d$ be the degree of its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$. If $d \ge 2$, then the algebraic Mahler measure $M(\alpha)$ satisfies $M(\alpha) > 1 + \frac{1}{52\, d \log(6d)}$, with $\log$ the natural logarithm.

results.title: Scottish Book Problem 176 (Eidelheit's claim)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The claim that in every complete normed ring $A$ (so $\|xy\| \le \|x\| \, \|y\|$, and $A$ has a unit) that is a normed algebra over $\mathbb{R}$, the inverse of every invertible element is a limit of real polynomials in that element: whenever $a, b \in A$ satisfy $ab = 1$ and $ba = 1$, there is a sequence $(p_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of real polynomials with $p_n(a) \to b$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Eidelheit's Problem 176 has a negative answer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The claim of Scottish Book Problem 176 is false: there are a complete normed ring $A$ that is a normed algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ and elements $a, b \in A$ with $ab = 1$ and $ba = 1$ such that $b$ is not the limit of any sequence $(p_n(a))_{n \ge 0}$ with $p_n$ real polynomials.

results.title: Finite Ramsey theorem for pairs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every number of colors $r \ge 1$ and every natural number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every coloring of the subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}$ with $r$ colors there are a $k$-element subset $S$ and a color $c$ such that every $2$-element subset of $S$ has color $c$.

results.title: Strengthened finite Ramsey theorem (Paris–Harrington principle)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all integers $c \ge 1$, $k \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every coloring $f$ of the finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ with $c$ colors there is a nonempty set $H \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ with $|H| \ge m$ and $\min H \le |H|$ such that all $k$-element subsets of $H$ have the same color: some color $t$ satisfies $f(S) = t$ for every $k$-element subset $S \subseteq H$.

results.title: Iterates of the substitution on $0$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $k \ge 0$, the word $\sigma^k(0)$ obtained from the one-letter word $0$ by applying the substitution $\sigma$ ($0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$) $k$ times, where $\sigma$ acts on a word by replacing each letter with its image: $\sigma^0(0) = 0$ and $\sigma^{k+1}(0) = \sigma(\sigma^k(0))$.

results.title: The fixed point generated from $0$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be the substitution $0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$, extended to words by replacing each letter with its image. An infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ is the fixed point generated from $0$ if the word $\sigma^k(0)$ is a prefix of $w$ for every $k \ge 0$.

results.title: Sum of a factor

results.title: Signed Stirling numbers of the first kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the signed Stirling number of the first kind is the integer $(-1)^{n-k} c(n,k)$, where $c(n,k)$ is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind (the number of permutations of $n$ elements with exactly $k$ cycles) and $n - k$ is truncated subtraction, equal to $0$ when $k > n$.

results.title: Number of cycles of a permutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of a finite type $\alpha$, the number of cycles of $\sigma$, counting each fixed point as a cycle of length one, is the number of equivalence classes of $\alpha$ under the relation that holds between $x$ and $y$ when $\sigma^i(x) = y$ for some integer $i$.

results.title: Counting cycles via the cycle type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of a finite type, the number of cycles of $\sigma$, counting each fixed point as a cycle of length one, equals the number of cycles of $\sigma$ of length at least $2$ (the length of its cycle type) plus the number of fixed points of $\sigma$.

results.title: Stirling numbers of the first kind count permutations by cycles
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the number of permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that the number of cycles of $\sigma$ of length at least $2$ plus the number of fixed points of $\sigma$ equals $k$ is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind $c(n, k)$. results.title: Non-symmetric peaks of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_\ell$ of natural numbers, a non-symmetric peak is a position $i$ with $1 < i < \ell$ such that $w_{i-1} < w_i$, $w_{i+1} < w_i$ and $w_{i-1} \ne w_{i+1}$. The non-symmetric peak count of $w$ is the number of such positions; in particular it is $0$ when $\ell < 3$.

results.title: Peaks of the word $1322141251$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The word $1322141251$ (the list $1, 3, 2, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1$) has exactly one symmetric peak, the factor $141$, and exactly two non-symmetric peaks, the factors $132$ and $251$.

results.title: The pushdown automaton simulating a context-free grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$, this is the pushdown automaton with input alphabet $T$, a single state, the terminals and nonterminals of $g$ as stack alphabet, and the initial nonterminal of $g$ as initial stack symbol. results.title: The grammar-simulating pushdown automaton accepts the grammar's language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context-free grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$, the language accepted by empty stack by the one-state pushdown automaton simulating $g$ equals the language generated by $g$.

results.title: Context-free languages are accepted by pushdown automata
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context-free language $L$ over an alphabet $T$ there are a context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and a pushdown automaton with input alphabet $T$, a single state, and the terminals and nonterminals of $g$ as stack alphabet, whose language accepted by empty stack is $L$.

results.title: The grammar-simulating pushdown automaton is finitely supported
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context-free grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$, the one-state pushdown automaton simulating $g$ is finitely supported.

results.title: Context-free languages are accepted by finitely supported pushdown automata
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context-free language $L$ over an alphabet $T$ there are a context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and a finitely supported pushdown automaton with input alphabet $T$, a single state, and the terminals and nonterminals of $g$ as stack alphabet, whose language accepted by empty stack is $L$.

results.title: Chain forms consist of nonterminals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of stack symbols and every list of states, every symbol of their chain form is a nonterminal.

results.title: Lists of states of a given length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $\sigma$ of states and a natural number $n$, this is the finite set of all lists of length $n$ with entries in $\sigma$. It is built recursively: for $n = 0$ it contains only the empty list, and for $n + 1$ it consists of the lists obtained by putting a state $p \in \sigma$ in front of a list from the set for $n$.

results.title: Terminal word of an optional input letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: As a word of grammar symbols (terminals and triple nonterminals), an input that is a letter $a$ contributes the one-symbol word consisting of the terminal $a$, and the empty input $\varepsilon$ contributes the empty word.

results.summary: Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a finite set of states, a finite stack alphabet, start state $q_0$ and initial stack symbol $Z_0$, and let $T_0$ be a finite set of input letters. results.title: The triple grammar generates the accepted language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and let $T_0$ be a finite set of input letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack symbol, that consumes a letter outside $T_0$. Then the language generated by the triple grammar of $M$ and $T_0$ equals the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack.

results.title: Finite pushdown automata accept context-free languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and suppose that there is a finite set $T_0$ of input letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack symbol, that consumes a letter outside $T_0$. Then the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack is context-free.

results.title: Context-free languages are exactly the languages of finite pushdown automata
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A language $L$ over an alphabet $T$ is context-free if and only if there are a pushdown automaton $M$ over $T$ with a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and a finite set $T_0$ of input letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack symbol, that consumes a letter outside $T_0$, for which the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack is $L$.
